meta.title: Who originally recorded "Hound Dog"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not an Elvis original. "Hound Dog" was first recorded by Big Mama Thornton in 1952 — a No. 1 R&B hit — and written by Jerry Leiber and Mike Stoller. Elvis Presley’s 1956 version is a cover.
meta.ogDescription: Everyone thinks it’s Elvis’s song. It’s a 1952 Big Mama Thornton record, written by two teenagers named Leiber and Stoller — and Elvis was copying a Las Vegas lounge parody of it.

answer.label: Not an Elvis original — a 1952 Big Mama Thornton record
answer.sourceLine: It is one of the most complete cover-eclipses in American music: almost everyone takes ‘Hound Dog’ for an Elvis Presley original, but Elvis’s 1956 version is a cover. The song was written by Jerry Leiber and Mike Stoller — both nineteen — and first recorded by Big Mama Thornton in 1952, whose record topped the R&B chart. Stranger still: Elvis wasn’t even copying Thornton. He was copying a lounge parody of her record by Freddie Bell and the Bellboys.

original.heading: Who recorded it first
original.label: Peacock Records (Peacock 1612)
original.charted: No. 1 on the US Billboard R&B chart in 1953; reportedly sold around half a million copies
original.cover: Elvis Presley — released 13 July 1956 on RCA Victor (RCA 6604). It hit No. 1 on the pop, country and R&B charts simultaneously and stayed atop the pop chart for eleven weeks, selling in the millions.
trail: The song was written by Jerry Leiber and Mike Stoller — both nineteen at the time — and first recorded by Big Mama Thornton on 13 August 1952, released the following February on Houston’s Peacock label Wikipedia ↗.

Unlike many eclipsed originals, Thornton’s record was a genuine hit: it reached No. 1 on the Billboard R&B chart in 1953. But it lived on the R&B side of a segregated music market, and did not cross into the mainstream pop audience that would later crown Elvis.

Elvis’s 1956 version was not even a direct cover of Thornton. He built his arrangement on a comic lounge parody performed by Freddie Bell and the Bellboys, which he saw in Las Vegas in 1955 — which is why his lyrics and tempo differ so much from the original SecondHandSongs ↗.

authors.name: Big Mama Thornton
authors.heading: About Big Mama Thornton
authors.bio: Willie Mae ‘Big Mama’ Thornton (1926–1984) was an Alabama-born blues singer with a growl that could fill a room. Her 1952 ‘Hound Dog’ was a No. 1 R&B hit, yet she is said to have earned only a few hundred dollars from it — and she wrote ‘Ball and Chain’, later a signature for Janis Joplin, to much the same fate. She is the person the song’s fame most thoroughly erased.

authors.name: Elvis Presley
authors.heading: Why it gets pinned on Elvis
authors.bio: Elvis Presley (1935–1977) released his ‘Hound Dog’ in 1956 and turned it into one of the biggest records of the decade — eleven weeks at No. 1. His version is genuinely his own performance, and a great one; the only error is chronological, assuming a 1956 juggernaut must be where the song began. It began in 1952, and he was working from a nightclub parody of it, not the source.

authors.name: Leiber and Stoller
authors.heading: About Leiber & Stoller
authors.metaLine: Jerry Leiber (1933–2011) & Mike Stoller (b. 1933) · American songwriting duo
authors.bio: Jerry Leiber and Mike Stoller wrote ‘Hound Dog’ as teenagers — both nineteen — before going on to write ‘Jailhouse Rock’, ‘Kansas City’, ‘Stand By Me’ and dozens more. They are the third party the song’s fame obscures: not the original singer, not the famous one, but the writers whose names most people never learn even after they’re told the record isn’t Elvis’s.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is a layered music misattribution: nothing about Elvis’s record is fake, but the belief that he originated ‘Hound Dog’ is wrong on two counts — there was an earlier hit, and even his arrangement came secondhand.

items.why: Elvis’s 1956 version is a cover. The song was recorded four years earlier, in 1952, by Big Mama Thornton the history ↗.

Her record hit No. 1 on the R&B chart — this was no forgotten B-side. It was eclipsed not because it flopped, but because it lived on the R&B side of a segregated market that white pop radio largely ignored.
Elvis based his tempo and reworked lyrics on the Bellboys’ 1955 Las Vegas lounge parody, not on Thornton’s original — so even his ‘version’ of the song was two steps removed from the source.

misattribution.truthLine: Written by Leiber and Stoller, first recorded by Big Mama Thornton in 1952, and made famous — but not originated — by Elvis Presley in 1956 the record ↗.

context.heading: Why the cover ate the original
lead: Most cover-eclipses happen because the original flopped. ‘Hound Dog’ is the harder case: Big Mama Thornton’s record was a No. 1 R&B hit, and it still got buried. It was buried by the racial geography of 1950s American radio, where a Black R&B smash and a white pop smash occupied almost separate worlds — and only one of them was remembered as ‘the’ version.

The detail people find hardest to believe is that Elvis wasn’t even reworking Thornton. He was reworking a comedy lounge act’s parody of her, glimpsed in Las Vegas. The song the world thinks of as Elvis’s is a cover of a parody of a record most listeners have never heard.
detailsBody: Leiber and Stoller write the song, 1952 — both aged nineteen.
Big Mama Thornton records it, 13 August 1952; released 1953 → No. 1 R&B.
Freddie Bell and the Bellboys turn it into a comic lounge number, 1955.
Elvis sees the Bellboys in Las Vegas and copies their arrangement.
Elvis records it, 1956 → No. 1 pop for eleven weeks; Thornton’s original fades from mainstream memory.
context.pull: The song the world thinks of as Elvis’s is a cover of a parody of a record most listeners have never heard.
